items.stem: In a fiction passage, which details usually reveal a character’s feelings most effectively?
items.answer: Their actions, speech and reactions
items.markingKey: Show, don’t tell: inference from behaviour.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’ the writer writes ‘Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up.’ What does ‘packed’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘filled’?
items.answer: ‘Packed’ suggests the aisle is filled to bursting, conveying the discomfort and chaos of the bus.
items.markingKey: Mark points: meaning in context (crushing overcrowding); effect beyond the plain alternative. Indicative: ‘Packed’ suggests the aisle is filled to bursting, conveying the discomfort and chaos of the bus.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the short story ‘The Audition’ the writer writes ‘The silence she left behind was enormous.’ What does ‘enormous’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘noticeable’?
items.answer: ‘Enormous’ makes the silence feel physically huge, as if it fills the corridor and presses on Tomás, conveying his rising anxiety.
items.markingKey: Mark points: meaning in context (overwhelming, oppressive quiet); effect beyond the plain alternative. Indicative: ‘Enormous’ makes the silence feel physically huge, as if it fills the corridor and presses on Tomás, conveying his rising anxiety.

items.stem: Timed practice (4 minutes) on the descriptive piece ‘Market Morning’. Extract: “A boy weaves between the stalls with a tower of bread rolls balanced on his head, never once looking up. … By noon the heat presses down like a hand, the shouting softens to murmurs and the traders doze beneath their awnings.” (a) What does ‘never once looking up’ suggest about the boy? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. (b) Give the meaning of ‘awnings’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) He is highly skilled and practised at carrying the bread; he does this every day. Evidence: ‘never once looking up’ – balancing a ‘tower’ without looking shows routine expertise. (b) Sheets of material stretched out to give shade.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: he is highly skilled and practised at carrying the bread; he does this every day. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘never once looking up’ (balancing a ‘tower’ without looking shows routine expertise) [2] (b) Sheets of material stretched out to give shade (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Timed practice (8 minutes) on the travel writing ‘Crossing the Salt Flats’. Extract: “Our driver, Luis, wore two pairs of sunglasses at once and still squinted. In the rainy season, he told us, a thin layer of water turns the flats into the world’s largest mirror, and the sky appears both above and below you. … There were no birds, no insects, no wind — only an enormous, humming emptiness.” (a) Give the meaning of ‘squinted’ as it is used in the text. (b) What happens to the flats in the rainy season? (c) Explain the effect of the word ‘humming’.
items.answer: (a) Looked with eyes partly closed. (b) A thin layer of water turns them into a huge mirror that reflects the sky. (c) ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises.
items.markingKey: (a) Looked with eyes partly closed (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) A thin layer of water turns them into a huge mirror that reflects the sky. [1] (c) 1 mark: meaning in context (a silence so deep it seems to make its own sound); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader; 1 mark: link to the wider impression created. Indicative: ‘Humming’ paradoxically gives the silence a faint sound, suggesting it is so total that the writer becomes aware of tiny internal noises. [3]

items.stem: Timed practice on a fiction or literary non-fiction passage: allow about 6 minutes. Read the descriptive piece ‘Market Morning’: “Before dawn the market is only shadows and voices. Then the first trader lifts her shutter with a clatter like a train, and the day begins. Within an hour the narrow lanes are crammed: baskets of glossy aubergines, pyramids of limes, buckets of silver fish still twitching in their shallow water. The air is thick with frying garlic and diesel. A boy weaves between the stalls with a tower of bread rolls balanced on his head, never once looking up. Old women haggle with the stallholders as if their lives depended on a few coins, then laugh and pay what was first asked. Scooters hiss and buzz along the edges like impatient insects. By noon the heat presses down like a hand, the shouting softens to murmurs and the traders doze beneath their awnings. The fish are gone. The limes are fewer. Only the flies remain busy, drawing lazy circles above the empty crates.” (a) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘the shouting softens to murmurs’. (b) Identify the technique used in ‘Only the flies remain busy, drawing lazy circles’ and explain its effect.
items.answer: (a) The loud noise of the market dies down to quiet talking. (b) Personification: the flies ‘drawing lazy circles’ are given human idleness, which captures the drowsy, finished mood of the afternoon.
items.markingKey: (a) The loud noise of the market dies down to quiet talking; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2] (b) 1 mark: personification; 1 mark for explaining the effect, e.g. the flies ‘drawing lazy circles’ are given human idleness, which captures the drowsy, finished mood of the afternoon. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the descriptive piece ‘Market Morning’ the writer writes ‘Within an hour the narrow lanes are crammed: baskets of glossy aubergines, pyramids of limes, buckets of silver fish still twitching in their shallow water.’ What does ‘twitching’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘lying’?
items.answer: ‘Twitching’ suggests the fish are still just alive, emphasising their freshness but also adding a vivid, slightly unsettling detail.
items.markingKey: Mark points: meaning in context (freshness and unsettling life); effect beyond the plain alternative. Indicative: ‘Twitching’ suggests the fish are still just alive, emphasising their freshness but also adding a vivid, slightly unsettling detail.

items.stem: Timed practice (4 minutes): in the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’ the writer writes ‘Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been.’ What does ‘cleared’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘cut down’?
items.answer: ‘Cleared’ is a neutral, business-like word that makes the destruction of a whole field of trees sound routine and quick; it contrasts with Grandfather’s slow, loving walk and shows how little the developers value the orchard.
items.markingKey: Mark points: meaning in context (quick, complete, business-like destruction); effect beyond the plain alternative. Indicative: ‘Cleared’ is a neutral, business-like word that makes the destruction of a whole field of trees sound routine and quick; it contrasts with Grandfather’s slow, loving walk and shows how little the developers value the orchard.

items.stem: Timed practice (4 minutes) on the short story ‘First Day at the Workshop’. Extract: “He was planing the edge of a door, his whole body leaning into each stroke, and long pale curls of wood spiralled to the floor around his boots. … I was not late; I was ten minutes early. … By the time I had finished, my arms ached and the floor gleamed, but he only grunted and handed me a piece of sandpaper and a scrap of rough timber.” (a) Identify the technique used in ‘long pale curls of wood spiralled to the floor’ and explain its effect. (b) Give the meaning of ‘grunted’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Visual imagery: the image of curls spiralling down shows the skill and rhythm of his planing, making his craftsmanship seem almost graceful. (b) Made a short, low sound instead of speaking.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: visual imagery; 1 mark for explaining the effect, e.g. the image of curls spiralling down shows the skill and rhythm of his planing, making his craftsmanship seem almost graceful. [2] (b) Made a short, low sound instead of speaking (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: When reading a report under timed conditions, which features help you find information fastest?
items.answer: Subheadings and topic sentences
items.markingKey: They signpost content.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the speech ‘Speech to the Youth Climate Forum’ the writer states ‘And that, I believe, is how we lose most things — not in a single disaster, but in small decisions that nobody notices.’ Explain whether ‘that, I believe, is how we lose most things’ is a fact or an opinion, and how it contributes to the writer’s viewpoint.
items.answer: It is an opinion – a judgement that could be disputed. It reveals the attitude that the writer is passionate but reasonable and hopeful.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: opinion with reason; 1 mark: link to viewpoint (passionate but reasonable and hopeful).

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’ the writer states ‘Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.’ Explain whether ‘Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.’ is a fact or an opinion, and how it contributes to the writer’s viewpoint.
items.answer: It is an opinion – a judgement that could be disputed. It reveals the attitude that the writer is critical of excessive, pointless homework but not of all homework.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: opinion with reason; 1 mark: link to viewpoint (critical of excessive, pointless homework but not of all homework).

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes) on the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’. Extract: “Confession: I used to check my phone 140 times a day. … Progress, not perfection.” Explain the effect of the ending / closing line in ‘Progress, not perfection.’.
items.answer: The short, memorable minor sentence sums up the message like a slogan.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies how the ending / closing line works here; 1 mark for its effect on pace, emphasis or meaning: the short, memorable minor sentence sums up the message like a slogan. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice (4 minutes) on the speech ‘Speech to the Youth Climate Forum’. Extract: “Friends, I want to begin with a number: eleven. … We measured the playground at midday in June: 41 degrees on the tarmac, 29 in the shade of that one remaining tree. … In twenty years, a pupil you will never meet will sit in their shade and not even think about it.” (a) How many trees were in the playground when the speaker’s mother was a pupil? (b) What does the speaker suggest is the real reward for planting trees? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) Eleven. (b) Helping future people who will benefit without knowing it; the action is unselfish. Evidence: ‘a pupil you will never meet will sit in their shade and not even think about it’ – ‘That is exactly the point’ shows the unnoticed benefit is the aim.
items.markingKey: (a) Eleven. [1] (b) 1 mark: helping future people who will benefit without knowing it; the action is unselfish. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘a pupil you will never meet will sit in their shade and not even think about it’ (‘That is exactly the point’ shows the unnoticed benefit is the aim) [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a non-fiction text: allow about 6 minutes. Read the opinion article ‘Should Homework Be Banned?’: “Every evening, in millions of homes, the same battle is fought over the kitchen table. Parents nag, children sulk, and a worksheet on fractions somehow takes two hours. It is time we asked whether homework is worth the misery. The evidence is far less clear than many teachers assume. Research suggests that for primary pupils homework makes little difference to achievement, while for older students modest amounts — around an hour a night — can help. Beyond that, the benefits fall away and stress rises. Yet many teenagers report three or more hours a night, squeezed in between sport, chores and part-time jobs. I am not arguing for banning homework altogether. Reading for pleasure, practising a musical instrument or revising for a test are valuable habits. What I object to is busywork: tasks set because a timetable says so, not because anyone will learn from them. Schools should set less homework, set it better and, above all, explain why it matters. Our children’s evenings are not an extension of the school day.” (a) According to the research, how much homework can help older students? (b) Give the meaning of ‘modest’ as it is used in the text. (c) Explain the effect of the opening hook in ‘Every evening, in millions of homes, the same battle is fought over the kitchen table.’.
items.answer: (a) Around an hour a night. (b) Moderate; not large. (c) Opening with a familiar domestic scene draws parents in by making the problem universal.
items.markingKey: (a) Around an hour a night. [1] (b) Moderate; not large (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (c) 1 mark: identifies how the opening hook works here; 1 mark for its effect on pace, emphasis or meaning: opening with a familiar domestic scene draws parents in by making the problem universal. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice (4 minutes): in the review ‘Review: The Floating Museum’ the writer states ‘Overall, though, this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds.’ Explain whether ‘this is a bold, imaginative museum that deserves its crowds’ is a fact or an opinion, and how it contributes to the writer’s viewpoint.
items.answer: It is an opinion – a judgement that could be disputed. It reveals the attitude that the writer is broadly enthusiastic, with honest reservations.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: opinion with reason; 1 mark: link to viewpoint (broadly enthusiastic, with honest reservations).

items.stem: Timed practice (6 minutes) on the leaflet ‘Visiting the Coral Reef Responsibly’. Extract: “It may look like rock, but it is a living animal, and a single touch can damage its delicate outer layer. … Many ordinary sun creams contain chemicals that bleach coral; ask at the visitor centre for approved brands. … Remember: take only photographs, leave only bubbles!” (a) Explain the effect of the word ‘living animal’. (b) Give the meaning of ‘bleach’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) calling coral a ‘living animal’ makes it a creature that can be hurt, prompting more care than ‘rock’ would. (b) Turn white by removing colour.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: meaning in context (a creature that can be hurt); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader; 1 mark: link to the wider impression created. Indicative: calling coral a ‘living animal’ makes it a creature that can be hurt, prompting more care than ‘rock’ would. [3] (b) Turn white by removing colour (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Timed practice on a non-fiction text: allow about 6 minutes. Read the blog ‘Street Food Fridays’: “Every Friday at six, the car park behind Colombo’s old railway station turns into the best restaurant in the city. No tables, no menus, no reservations — just thirty-odd stalls, a few strings of coloured bulbs and a crowd that grows until you can barely move. My first stop is always Ravi’s kottu stall, where two flat-topped grills clatter like a drum band as he chops roti, egg and vegetables together with a pair of steel blades. A plate costs less than a bus ticket. Next, I queue for hoppers: crisp, bowl-shaped pancakes with a soft egg at the centre. I have burned my fingers on them every single week and I regret nothing. Not everything is perfect. There are not enough bins, and by nine the ground is littered with paper plates. But the council has promised more bins from next month, and the traders now run a tidy-up rota. Come hungry, bring cash, and wear shoes you don’t mind ruining.” (a) Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘wear shoes you don’t mind ruining’. (b) Explain the effect of the word ‘littered’.
items.answer: (a) Wear old shoes because they may get dirty or damaged. (b) ‘Littered’ suggests rubbish scattered carelessly everywhere, giving an honest, unglamorous picture of the market.
items.markingKey: (a) Wear old shoes because they may get dirty or damaged; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2] (b) 1 mark: meaning in context (messy neglect); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Littered’ suggests rubbish scattered carelessly everywhere, giving an honest, unglamorous picture of the market. [2]

items.stem: How long is Paper 1 (Reading) in this course?
items.answer: 2 hours
items.markingKey: Paper 1 (Reading) lasts 2 hours and carries 80 marks: four compulsory questions of 20 marks each (comprehension, summary, language task, extended response).

items.stem: How many marks does Paper 1 carry in total?
items.markingKey: Paper 1 (Reading) lasts 2 hours and carries 80 marks: four compulsory questions of 20 marks each (comprehension, summary, language task, extended response).

items.stem: Explain why it is unwise to spend 50 minutes on the first 20-mark question of a 2-hour, 80-mark paper.
items.answer: The fair share is about 30 minutes; overrunning leaves too little time for the later questions, where easy marks may be lost.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: fair share ≈ 30 min (20 × 1.5); 1 mark: consequence for later questions. [2]

items.stem: A student plans their time for Paper 1 (120 minutes, 80 marks). They allow 15 minutes to read the passages and 10 minutes at the end to check. The four questions carry 20, 20, 20 and 20 marks. Calculate, to the nearest minute, how long the student should spend on each question.
items.answer: Q1: 24 min, Q2: 24 min, Q3: 24 min, Q4: 24 min
items.markingKey: marks × time per mark, e.g. 20 × 1.19 ≈ 24 [2]

items.stem: Paper 1 (Reading) lasts 2 hours and carries 80 marks: four compulsory questions of 20 marks each (comprehension, summary, language task, extended response). A student read the passages for 15 minutes and then spent 38 minutes on Question 1. There are 67 minutes left for Questions 2, 3 and 4 (20 marks each). (a) Calculate, to the nearest minute, the time for each remaining question. (b) Suggest and justify a strategy for the remaining time.
items.answer: (a) about 22 minutes each (b) Plan the summary and extended response briefly, cover every bullet or focus point at least briefly, and stick strictly to the new time per question; partial answers to all questions earn more than a perfect answer to one.
items.markingKey: (a) 20 × 1.12 ≈ 22 [1] (b) sensible, justified strategy [2]

items.stem: A student plans their time for Paper 1 (120 minutes, 80 marks). They allow 15 minutes to read the passages. The four questions carry 20, 15, 25 and 20 marks. (a) Calculate the time available for writing answers. (b) Calculate the time available per mark. (c) Explain why the student should still move on if a question is unfinished when its time is up.
items.answer: (a) 105 minutes (b) 1.31 minutes (c) Later questions carry marks that are easier to gain at the start of an answer than the last marks of an overrun one.
items.markingKey: (a) 120 − 15 = 105 [1] (b) 105 ÷ 80 = 1.31 min per mark [1] (c) diminishing returns / later marks [1]

items.answer: R4
items.markingKey: R4: demonstrate understanding of how writers achieve effects and influence readers.

items.stem: Which reading objective is mainly tested by this task? “Explain the effect of the simile ‘like a shield’.”
items.answer: R4

items.stem: ‘In my letter in role I retold the passage in order and did not add anything.’ Identify the reading objective this comment shows weakness in, explain the problem and suggest a target.
items.answer: R3 (analyse, evaluate and develop facts, ideas and opinions, using appropriate support from the text): ideas were not developed or evaluated. Target: Infer motives, feelings and consequences from details and comment on them in role.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: R3; 1 mark: explanation (ideas were not developed or evaluated.); further mark: specific target (Infer motives, feelings and consequences from details and comment on them in role.).

items.stem: In a practice Paper 1 (four questions, 20 marks each), a student scored: Q1 comprehension 16/20, Q2 summary 9/20, Q3 language task 7/20, Q4 extended response 8/20. (a) Calculate the percentage for each question. (b) Suggest one specific target to improve that question.
items.answer: (a) Q1 80%, Q2 45%, Q3 35%, Q4 40% (b) Choose precise words/images and explain meaning, connotation and effect.
items.markingKey: (a) each mark ÷ 20 × 100 [1] (b) specific, relevant target [1]

items.stem: A student’s Paper 1 marks are broken down by objective: Q1 retrieval 5/10 (R1), Q1 inference 5/10 (R2), Q2 summary content 6/10 (R5), Q3 language task 8/20 (R4), Q4 reading 9/10 (R3). (a) Convert each score to a percentage. (b) Identify the two weakest objectives.
items.answer: (a) R1 (Q1 retrieval) 50%, R2 (Q1 inference) 50%, R5 (Q2 summary content) 60%, R4 (Q3 language) 40%, R3 (Q4 reading) 90% (b) R4 (Q3 language) and R1 (Q1 retrieval)
items.markingKey: (a) all five correct [2] (b) R4 (Q3 language); R1 (Q1 retrieval) [1]

items.stem: In a practice Paper 1 (four questions, 20 marks each), a student scored: Q1 comprehension 8/20, Q2 summary 16/20, Q3 language task 15/20, Q4 extended response 9/20. (a) Calculate the total mark and the overall percentage. (b) Suggest one specific target to improve that question.
items.answer: (a) 48/80 = 60% (b) Answer to the mark allocation: point + evidence for inference questions; precise detail for retrieval.

items.stem: Literary non-fiction differs from a short story because it
options: is always written in the future tense
describes real experiences, often using literary techniques
items.answer: describes real experiences, often using literary techniques
items.markingKey: E.g. memoir, travel writing.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the memoir ‘My Grandmother’s Kitchen’ the writer writes ‘For years my attempts were either bland or so fiery that my friends wept.’ What does ‘wept’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘coughed’?
items.answer: ‘Wept’ exaggerates the effect of the spice to comic effect, showing how badly the writer’s attempts went wrong.
items.markingKey: Mark points: meaning in context (comic exaggeration of the spice); effect beyond the plain alternative. Indicative: ‘Wept’ exaggerates the effect of the spice to comic effect, showing how badly the writer’s attempts went wrong.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes) on the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’. Extract: “The road climbed in hairpin bends, and on the outside of each bend there was nothing at all — no barrier, no verge, only a sheer drop to a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below. … Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread and pressed it into my hand, then pointed out of the window at a line of snow peaks that had appeared above the clouds.” What does this action suggest about the woman beside the writer? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: She is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss. Evidence: ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread’ – ‘The woman beside me noticed’ the white knuckles.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: she is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread’ (‘The woman beside me noticed’ the white knuckles) [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a fiction or literary non-fiction passage: allow about 6 minutes. Read the short story ‘The Night Ferry’: “The ferry left the harbour at nine, an hour late, because the captain refused to cast off until the last delivery van had rattled up the ramp. Mira found a seat on the open deck, her rucksack wedged between her ankles like a nervous dog. Within minutes the lights of the town had shrunk to a smudge, and then the fog swallowed them completely. The engine throbbed beneath her feet. Somewhere below, a child was crying and a radio crackled out a song she half remembered from her grandmother’s kitchen. Mira pulled her scarf tighter. She had told her mother she would be fine travelling alone; she had said it three times, as if repeating it would make it true. Now, with nothing but grey in every direction, she checked her ticket again. Island of Sela, arrival 08:55. Twelve hours. She could manage twelve hours. A deckhand passed, whistling, and nodded at her as though night crossings were the most ordinary thing in the world. For him, she supposed, they were.” (a) Explain the effect of the word ‘crackled’. (b) Explain the effect of the minor sentence in ‘Island of Sela, arrival 08:55.’.
items.answer: (a) ‘Crackled’ suggests a poor signal and a faint, broken song, which matches the half-remembered memory of her grandmother and makes home seem far away. (b) The verbless sentence copies the words on the ticket, focusing the reader on how far she still has to go.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: meaning in context (a weak, distant, broken sound); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Crackled’ suggests a poor signal and a faint, broken song, which matches the half-remembered memory of her grandmother and makes home seem far away. [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies how the minor sentence works here; 1 mark for its effect on pace, emphasis or meaning: the verbless sentence copies the words on the ticket, focusing the reader on how far she still has to go. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a fiction or literary non-fiction passage: allow about 8 minutes. Read the short story ‘The Audition’: “The corridor outside Room 4 was lined with plastic chairs, and on every chair sat someone more talented than Tomás. At least, that was how it felt. The girl beside him was tuning her cello with tiny, confident twists of the pegs, humming the note under her breath. Tomás held his violin case on his knees like a shield. He had practised the Bach every morning for six months, before school, before breakfast, before his little brothers were awake to complain. He knew every bar. But now his fingers felt like they belonged to somebody else — stiff, cold, clumsy. A door opened. A man with a clipboard read out a name that was not his, and the cellist rose and glided away. The silence she left behind was enormous. Tomás closed his eyes and pictured the kitchen at home, the grey light at six o’clock, his mother pretending to sleep through his scales. When the man returned and said ‘Tomás Ferreira?’, he was surprised to find that his hands had stopped shaking.” (a) For how long had Tomás practised the Bach? (b) Where were the candidates waiting? (c) What does this detail suggest about Tomás’s mother? Use evidence from the text to support your answer.
items.answer: (a) Every morning for six months. (b) In the corridor outside Room 4. (c) She is patient and supportive; she puts up with the early-morning noise to encourage him. Evidence: ‘his mother pretending to sleep through his scales’ – ‘pretending’ shows she is awake but chooses not to complain.
items.markingKey: (a) Every morning for six months. [1] (b) In the corridor outside Room 4. [1] (c) 1 mark: she is patient and supportive; she puts up with the early-morning noise to encourage him. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘his mother pretending to sleep through his scales’ (‘pretending’ shows she is awake but chooses not to complain) 1 mark: developed explanation of how the evidence shows this [3]

items.stem: Timed practice (1 minute) on the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’: ‘The floodlights now stay on until 2 a.m., seven nights a week, even though the park closes at ten.’ When does the park close?
items.answer: At ten o’clock.
items.markingKey: At ten o’clock.

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the magazine article ‘The Return of the Urban Beekeeper’ the writer states ‘In fact, it’s often better than country honey.’ Explain whether ‘it’s often better than country honey’ is a fact or an opinion, and how it contributes to the writer’s viewpoint.
items.answer: It is an opinion – a judgement that could be disputed. It reveals the attitude that the writer is broadly positive about urban beekeeping but balanced.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: opinion with reason; 1 mark: link to viewpoint (broadly positive about urban beekeeping but balanced).

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes) on the blog ‘Why I Gave Up My Smartphone for a Month’. Extract: “The first week was horrible. … Honestly, yes; I need it for work.” Explain the effect of the word ‘horrible’.
items.answer: ‘Horrible’ is blunt and informal, showing honestly how hard the first week was and making the later benefits more believable.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (blunt, informal admission of difficulty); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Horrible’ is blunt and informal, showing honestly how hard the first week was and making the later benefits more believable. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a non-fiction text: allow about 6 minutes. Read the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’: “Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven. Of the 1,400 homes flooded, around 900 have been repaired and reoccupied. The remaining families are still living with relatives or in temporary housing at the sports centre. The main road bridge, which was closed after cracks were found in its supports, reopened last week following emergency repairs costing 2.3 million dollars. However, the district’s only secondary school remains shut, and around 600 students are being taught in shifts at a primary school four kilometres away. Local businesses have been hit hard. A survey by the traders’ association found that one in five shops has not reopened, and many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage. Engineers have recommended raising the flood wall by one metre and restoring wetlands upstream to slow the water in future. The regional government says it will publish its decision by the end of the year.” (a) How much did the emergency bridge repairs cost? (b) What does this suggest about why some shops have not reopened? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. (c) Give the meaning of ‘upstream’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) 2.3 million dollars. (b) The owners cannot afford the repairs without insurance money. Evidence: ‘many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage’ – no insurance payout means no money for repairs. (c) Further up a river, towards its source.
items.markingKey: (a) 2.3 million dollars. [1] (b) 1 mark: the owners cannot afford the repairs without insurance money. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘many owners say their insurance did not cover flood damage’ (no insurance payout means no money for repairs) [2] (c) Further up a river, towards its source (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the diary ‘Turtle Hatchery Diary’ the writer writes ‘My back is aching as I write this.’ What does ‘aching’ suggest, and why is it more effective than ‘tired’?

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes) on the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’. Extract: “Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up. … I gripped the seat in front so hard my knuckles turned white.” Explain the effect of the word ‘gripped’.
items.answer: ‘Gripped’ suggests a tight, desperate hold, showing the writer’s terror on the mountain road.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: meaning in context (tense, fearful clinging); 1 mark: connotation/effect on the reader. Indicative: ‘Gripped’ suggests a tight, desperate hold, showing the writer’s terror on the mountain road. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a fiction or literary non-fiction passage: allow about 6 minutes. Read the travel writing ‘The Bus to Kathmandu’: “The bus was supposed to leave at seven. It left at nine, after the driver had finished his tea, his second tea and a long conversation with a man selling oranges. Every seat was taken, and the aisle was soon packed with sacks of rice, a crate of hens and a schoolboy who fell asleep standing up. The road climbed in hairpin bends, and on the outside of each bend there was nothing at all — no barrier, no verge, only a sheer drop to a river that glittered like a thread of tin far below. I gripped the seat in front so hard my knuckles turned white. The woman beside me noticed. Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread and pressed it into my hand, then pointed out of the window at a line of snow peaks that had appeared above the clouds. For a moment I forgot to be afraid. We arrived eleven hours later, stiff, dusty and somehow friends.” (a) At what time did the bus actually leave? (b) What does this action suggest about the woman beside the writer? Use evidence from the text to support your answer. (c) Give the meaning of ‘sheer’ as it is used in the text.
items.answer: (a) Nine o’clock. (b) She is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss. Evidence: ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread’ – ‘The woman beside me noticed’ the white knuckles. (c) Extremely steep, almost vertical.
items.markingKey: (a) Nine o’clock. [1] (b) 1 mark: she is kind and perceptive; she sees the writer’s fear and offers comfort without fuss. 1 mark: supporting evidence, e.g. ‘Without a word, she broke a piece from her bread’ (‘The woman beside me noticed’ the white knuckles) [2] (c) Extremely steep, almost vertical (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1]

items.stem: Timed practice on a fiction or literary non-fiction passage: allow about 8 minutes. Read the short story ‘The Last Mango Tree’: “Grandfather walked the orchard every evening, even after the land had been sold. He moved slowly between the rows, touching each trunk as if he were taking attendance at a school register. Most of the trees were already gone; the developers had cleared the eastern field in a single week, and now orange flags fluttered where the guavas had been. Only the old mango by the well remained. ‘Planted it the year your mother was born,’ he told me, though I had heard the story a hundred times. Its bark was cracked like a dry riverbed, and its lowest branch dipped so close to the ground that I could sit on it without jumping. That evening he did not speak for a long while. He pressed his palm flat against the trunk and kept it there. Then he took out his pocket knife, cut a single green mango and handed it to me. ‘Keep the stone,’ he said. ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’” (a) Give the meaning of ‘fluttered’ as it is used in the text. (b) Identify the technique used in ‘as if he were taking attendance at a school register’ and explain its effect. (c) Explain the effect of the ending / closing line in ‘Plant it somewhere they can’t reach.’.
items.answer: (a) Moved lightly and quickly in the wind. (b) Simile: comparing Grandfather to a teacher calling the register suggests care, responsibility and routine; it also makes the missing trees feel like absent pupils. (c) The passage ends on Grandfather’s instruction, leaving the reader with defiance and hope rather than only loss.
items.markingKey: (a) Moved lightly and quickly in the wind (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) 1 mark: simile; 1 mark for explaining the effect, e.g. comparing Grandfather to a teacher calling the register suggests care, responsibility and routine; it also makes the missing trees feel like absent pupils. [2] (c) 1 mark: identifies how the ending / closing line works here; 1 mark for its effect on pace, emphasis or meaning: the passage ends on Grandfather’s instruction, leaving the reader with defiance and hope rather than only loss. [2]

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes): in the news article ‘Flood Recovery in the River District’ the writer states ‘Three months after the River Kali burst its banks, recovery in the River District is uneven.’ Explain whether ‘recovery in the River District is uneven’ is a fact or an opinion, and how it contributes to the writer’s viewpoint.
items.answer: It is an opinion – a judgement that could be disputed. It reveals the attitude that the writer is largely neutral and factual, with a quiet note of concern.
items.markingKey: Mark points: 1 mark: opinion with reason; 1 mark: link to viewpoint (largely neutral and factual, with a quiet note of concern).

items.stem: Timed practice (3 minutes) on the letter to a newspaper ‘Protect Our Night Sky’. Extract: “The floodlights now stay on until 2 a.m., seven nights a week, even though the park closes at ten. … Light pollution is not merely a hobby problem for people like me.” Explain, using your own words, what the writer means by ‘not merely a hobby problem’.
items.answer: Not only an issue for people who enjoy stargazing.
items.markingKey: Not only an issue for people who enjoy stargazing; 1 mark for each clear element of the meaning, in own words; repeating the original words gains no credit [2]

items.stem: Timed practice on a non-fiction text: allow about 6 minutes. Read the interview ‘The Mountain Rescue Volunteer’: “Sipho Ndlovu has been called out 212 times in eleven years with the Drakensberg mountain rescue team, and he still keeps his boots by the front door. ‘The phone can ring at three in the morning,’ he says. ‘You have perhaps ten minutes to be in the truck.’ Like the rest of the team, he is an unpaid volunteer; by day he teaches mathematics at a local secondary school. Most call-outs, he explains, are not dramatic falls but simple mistakes: hikers who set off too late, who underestimate how quickly the weather changes, or who rely on a phone battery that dies on the mountain. The worst night he remembers was a search for two teenagers in thick cloud. ‘We found them at dawn, cold and frightened but alive. I have never been so tired or so happy.’ Asked why he continues, he shrugs. ‘Someone came for my father once, years ago. I suppose I am paying it back.’” (a) Give the meaning of ‘unpaid’ as it is used in the text. (b) Using your own words, list three points the text makes about the common mistakes that lead to rescues and what volunteering involves.
items.answer: (a) Not receiving money for work. (b) Hikers start too late; They underestimate sudden weather changes; They rely on phones whose batteries fail.
items.markingKey: (a) Not receiving money for work (accept close synonyms that fit the context) [1] (b) 1 mark per point in own words [3]
